title: "Colour in Slides: Building a Palette That Works on Screen" (blog explainer)

brief.story: A clear explainer of the post.

slides.title: Building a Palette That Works on Screen
slides.notes: Colour can make a deck look considered, or make it look messy. Here's how to build a small palette that reads well on laptops, phones and in video.

slides.title: Why Most Slide Palettes Go Wrong
slides.notes: Most slide palettes trip over the same things. There are too many colours and brand colours everywhere. Contrast is weak, and colour carries meaning on its own.

slides.title: Think in Roles, Not Favourite Colours
slides.notes: Think in roles, not favourite colours. Pick a background, text colours, a couple of greys, one accent for what matters and a quiet support colour. That's five to seven in total.

slides.title: Test Contrast Before You Commit
slides.notes: Colours that look fine on your monitor can wash out on a projector. Aim for 4.5 to 1 contrast for body text, and label your chart series directly.

slides.title: One Accent Makes the Chart Speak
bullets: Before: six bars, six brand colours
After: five bars in light grey
The north bar in the accent
slides.notes: Take a chart with six bars in six brand colours. Grey out five, put the north in the accent, and the slide says exactly one thing.

slides.title: Make Your Palette Work in Video
bullets: Preview on a phone and in the finished video
slides.notes: On Pro, a.i. directs your video, rebuilding charts as animated charts and landing your accent on the word that names it. Try Basic first at powerpoint2vid.com.
